content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler multiple fruit, Stage 2 (item 4113) is infant food for babies aged 6‑12 months. The puree blends apple, pear, banana and peach, prepared without added sugar, salt or preservatives. It meets Stage 2 requirements, providing a gradual transition from single‑fruit to more varied flavors.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The four‑fruit blend delivers a broad spectrum of vitamins and minerals.
All fruits are sourced from certified regions following organic farming standards.
The puree is cooked at low temperature to preserve maximum nutrients.
Packaging is BPA‑free, microwave‑safe plastic.
The product has undergone clinical tolerance testing in infants 6‑12 months old.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Fruits are rich in vitamin C, which supports the immune system and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Dietary Fiber
items.content: The puree contains soluble and insoluble fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Folate
items.content: Folate is essential for growth and nervous system development in infants.

items.title: Low Sugar Content
items.content: No added sugar helps establish healthy taste preferences early on.

items.title: Fruit Allergy
items.content: Some children may be allergic to one of the components (apple, pear, banana, peach). Observe the child closely at first introduction.

items.title: Choking Hazard
items.content: The puree must be completely smooth, without large pieces, to avoid choking risk.

items.title: Storage After Opening
items.content: Once opened, keep the container refrigerated and use within 48 hours.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The puree is ready to eat straight from the pack. If desired, gently warm in the microwave (no more than 30 seconds) and stir. It can be mixed into cereal or yogurt for added variety.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place at 5 °C‑25 °C. After opening, refrigerate and consume within 48 hours. Discard if the package is damaged or the product has an off‑odor.

content.title: About
content.content: Woven wheat crackers with reduced sodium are crisp, dry biscuits made from whole‑grain wheat. They contain only about 150 mg of sodium per 100 g, making them suitable for low‑salt diets. The flavor is mild with a slight nutty note, and the texture is crunchy and flaky.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The woven technique creates a distinctive pattern and a more uniform crumb structure.
Sodium reduction is achieved by using natural herbs and spices instead of added salt.
Whole‑grain wheat retains more fiber and B‑vitamins than refined white crackers.
The product does not contain added gluten‑free agents, but it does contain gluten from the wheat itself.
Packaging is typically recyclable, reducing environmental impact.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain wheat provides fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: Reduced salt helps control blood pressure and eases kidney load.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Crackers deliver sustained energy through slow‑release glucose.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B3 and B6 aid metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: A 30 g serving provides roughly 120 kcal, fitting well into calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: People with wheat allergy or celiac disease should avoid this product.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: Not suitable for gluten‑free diets.

items.title: Additive sensitivity
items.content: Some variants may contain preservatives or flavorings that could affect sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the crackers as a snack, pair them with low‑fat cottage cheese, hummus, avocado spread, or use them as a base for canapés. They are convenient to pack in a bag or backpack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in an airtight bag or container. For longer storage (over 3 months) keep refrigerated to maintain crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Danish pastry is a laminated sweet pastry made from a yeast‑leavened dough enriched with butter. The “plain” version is a buttery, flaky layer without filling, while the “spice” version incorporates aromatic spices such as cinnamon, cardamom, and ginger.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The pastry originated in 19th‑century Denmark, inspired by Austrian “Viennese” pastries.
Traditional lamination creates over 100 layers by repeatedly rolling and folding the dough.
In the United States the product is often simply called “pastry” or “Danish”.
There are more than 30 common fillings, ranging from fruit jams to almond cream and caramel.
In some Danish regions the pastry is served warm with milk as a breakfast staple.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Provides carbohydrates and a modest amount of fat for quick energy.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Yeast‑based dough supplies thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants (Spice version)
items.content: Spices like cinnamon and ginger contain polyphenols that may reduce oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Whole‑grain flour, when used, adds dietary fiber that aids bowel regularity.

items.title: Mood improvement
items.content: Carbohydrates promote serotonin production, which can enhance mood.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Fillings and sweetened dough can raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Possible trans fats
items.content: Using margarine instead of butter may introduce trans fatty acids.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Contains milk, eggs, gluten, and sometimes nuts, which can trigger allergies.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The buttery layers make the pastry calorie‑rich; moderation is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy Danish pastry as a standalone treat, sliced and paired with coffee or tea. The spice‑infused version pairs especially well with hot milk or a scoop of vanilla ice cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container at room temperature for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate (up to 5 days) or freeze (up to 2 months). Reheat in the oven before serving to restore crispness.

egg-roll-with-chicken-or-turkey.title: Egg roll with chicken or turkey

content.title: About
content.content: Egg roll is a crispy roll made from thin dough, filled with tender chicken or turkey meat, vegetables, and aromatic spices. The dough is fried to a golden crust while the filling stays juicy and flavorful.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Egg roll originates from Asian street food culture and is commonly served in food stalls.
The turkey version was created as a leaner alternative to the traditional chicken filling.
The dough is a simple mixture of flour, water and salt, without eggs.
Traditionally the rolls are served with soy sauce, sweet chili or vinegar.
Some regional recipes add finely diced pineapple for a subtle sweetness.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey provide complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in fat (turkey)
items.content: Turkey contains less saturated fat than chicken, making it a better choice for low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Poultry is rich in B3 and B6 vitamins, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It supplies iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for blood health and bones.

items.title: Vegetable content
items.content: Added vegetables (cabbage, carrot, onion) provide fiber, vitamins and antioxidants.

items.title: Allergy to chicken/turkey
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to poultry, experiencing skin reactions or digestive issues.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce used in preparation can raise the salt level; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Trans fats in fried dough
items.content: Deep‑frying can create trans fats; choosing rolls fried in low‑temperature vegetable oil reduces this risk.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The crispy dough makes the roll energy‑dense; moderation is advised for weight‑management diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Egg roll is convenient to eat by hand as a snack or light meal. Serve it with soy sauce, sweet chili, vinegar, or a yogurt‑based dipping sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep prepared rolls in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in the oven or skillet to restore crispness before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Egg white is the clear liquid surrounding the yolk of a chicken egg. Raw egg white is about 90 % water and 10 % proteins, including albumin, ovalbumin and lysozyme. It contains virtually no fat or carbohydrates and very little vitamins or minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Egg white is composed of roughly 90 % water.
It provides all essential amino acids, making it a complete protein source.
Raw egg white is used in cooking to create airy meringues and soufflés.
When heated, the proteins coagulate, turning the clear liquid into a white, firm mass.
Lysozyme in egg white has antibacterial properties.

items.title: High‑quality protein source
items.content: Egg white supplies the body with all essential amino acids, supporting tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat and calories
items.content: Because it contains virtually no fat, egg white is suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Contains lysozyme
items.content: Lysozyme exhibits antibacterial activity and may help support the immune system.

items.title: Supports muscle mass
items.content: The abundant protein aids muscle protein synthesis, especially beneficial for active individuals.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: Egg white contains very little sodium, making it a good choice for those monitoring salt intake.

items.title: Risk of salmonella
items.content: Raw egg white can be contaminated with Salmonella bacteria; using pasteurized eggs or cooking it is recommended.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Egg white is a common allergen and can cause reactions ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Lack of vitamins and minerals
items.content: Because it contains almost no vitamins or minerals, relying solely on egg white for nutrition is not advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw egg white is frequently used in culinary applications such as meringues, soufflés, protein shakes, and baked goods. When consuming raw, choose pasteurized eggs to reduce infection risk.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep eggs refrigerated at 1‑4 °C. Separated raw egg white should be used within 2‑3 days or frozen in an airtight container for up to 3 months.

mustard-greens-fresh-cooked-fat-added.title: Mustard greens, fresh, cooked, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: Mustard greens (Brassica juncea) are edible leafy vegetables commonly used in Asian cuisine. When cooked with added fat, they retain a bright flavor and become tender. They are rich in vitamins A, C, K and minerals such as calcium and iron.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mustard greens belong to the cruciferous family, along with broccoli and cabbage.
The seeds are used to make spicy mustard, while the leaves are enjoyed in salads and side dishes.
In traditional Indian cooking, the leaves are often stir‑fried with oil and spices.
Glucosinolates in mustard greens may support liver detoxification.
Leafy greens lose nutrients quickly during storage, so they are best cooked soon after purchase.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C provides antioxidant protection and enhances iron absorption.

items.title: Source of vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains calcium and iron
items.content: These minerals are important for bones, teeth, and oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Low‑calorie source of fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Glucosinolates content
items.content: In large amounts they can irritate the gastrointestinal tract in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Cruciferous allergy
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to mustard greens.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Those prone to kidney stones should consume mustard greens in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The leaves can be quickly stir‑fried in a small amount of oil with garlic, ginger, and soy sauce. They also work well in soups, stews, and mixed vegetable dishes. Freshly prepared greens make a vibrant side for rice or quinoa.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh leaves in the refrigerator in a perforated bag with a slight moisture to stay crisp for 3–5 days. Cooked greens with added fat should be eaten within 2 days, stored in an airtight container.

content.title: About
content.content: Refried beans are a ready‑to‑eat product made from cooked and mashed beans, usually pinto or black beans, seasoned with spices and cooked to a creamy consistency. This version is packaged in a can with reduced sodium (2166 mg per serving), making it more suitable for low‑salt diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Refried beans are a staple of Mexican cuisine and are often served as a side dish for tacos and burritos.
Canned beans have a long shelf life and do not require refrigeration until opened.
The reduced‑sodium formulation is achieved by using lower‑salt blends and flavor enhancers.
Beans are an excellent source of plant protein and dietary fiber.
Traditional recipes often fry the beans in butter, but many canned versions use vegetable oils.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Beans provide about 7 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance and satiety.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber aids digestion, helps regulate blood sugar, and supports heart health.

items.title: Reduced sodium
items.content: Lower salt content makes the product more suitable for people monitoring blood pressure.

items.title: Source of iron and magnesium
items.content: Iron contributes to hemoglobin formation, while magnesium supports muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Beans are rich in polyphenols, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans, ranging from skin rashes to severe symptoms.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce the absorption of certain minerals; varied diet helps mitigate this effect.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Beans can cause gastrointestinal gas in sensitive people; introduce them gradually.

items.title: Added sugars
items.content: Some canned varieties may contain added sugar; check the label if you monitor sugar intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the refried beans in the microwave or on the stove, add them to tacos, burritos, chili, soups, or use as a dip for nachos. They pair well with cheese, avocado, salsa, and fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened can in a cool, dry place. After opening, keep the beans in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. Discard if the product develops off‑odors, discoloration, or off‑flavors.

content.title: About
content.content: Spanish rice is a long‑grain variety traditionally used in Spanish cuisine, especially in paella. It has a subtle aromatic flavor, absorbs sauces well, and holds its shape during cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The rice used for paella is often called “balsa” and is cultivated in the Valencia and Catalonia regions.
Traditional paella preparation avoids stirring the rice so that a crust called “socarrat” forms at the bottom.
Spanish rice has a higher amylopectin content, making it slightly stickier than ordinary long‑grain rice.
In Spain, rice is considered a key part of the national culinary heritage and is protected by a geographical indication.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice provides sustained energy through slowly digestible carbs.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: It contains less than 1 g of fat per 100 g, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, which support metabolism.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Rice provides magnesium and phosphorus, important for muscle and bone health.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Rice can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Arsenic in raw grains
items.content: Some rice varieties may contain trace arsenic; choose reputable brands and rinse well before cooking.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Spanish rice is perfect for paella, risotto, salads, and side dishes. Cook it in broth, add vegetables, seafood or meat. Rinse the rice before cooking to remove excess starch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For long‑term storage, keep it in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent pest infestation.
